author: The Idea Guide
title: Visiting The Tech Washout
text:
by Daniel Shvartsman
It's Thanksgiving week in U.S. markets, a three-day week followed by binging on turkey and then a half-hearted day of trading. This may come as a relief to markets, which have had a bumpy Q4 as you no doubt already know.
^IXIC data by YCharts
Tech and small-caps (represented by the Nasdaq and the Russell 2000) have done worst in the recent pullback. Are we at the point of a washout, or are tech names stuck in the no-man's land between growth and value? This Idea Guide, pulling from articles published from November 9th-November 15th, looks at a few smaller tech names to see what the case is on both the long and short side.
Long Ideas We published 231 long ideas in the week in question, with stories on Apple ( AAPL ), General Electric ( GE ), and the usual big tech names like Nvidia ( NVDA ) and AMD ( AMD ) dominating reader attention. But there were a few mid or small-cap names that stood out.
Zillow's Price 50% Off. Time To Buy? by From Growth to Value Zillow ( Z ) ( ZG ) is an example of how widespread the 'tech' sector and the software as a service (SaaS) model and mindset spreads, and also how it's hard to keep track of all of these names. The stock was a sensation 4-5 years ago, it feels like, but here it still is, with a nearly $6B market cap. That comes after the stock has fallen in half in 2018.
From Growth to Value pins the sell-off on distaste over Zillow's move into acquiring and selling houses, and over distrust of the company's growth in its main revenue line, Premier Agents. The author takes the company's explanation for both issues as reasonable. The house-flipping business rationale is interesting to me - CEO Spencer Rascoff has been calling it a move akin to Netflix's ( NFLX ) move to original content. It's an interesting comparison. I think where it matches is that a) Netflix and Zillow both have data advantages that would appear to give them an edge, and b) they are both leveraging up their exposure to their core market. Which, I guess, is smart and risky - if you think you're going to win, you may as well bet big. The risky side is if you can't gain economies of scale, something Professor Aswath Damodaran pointed out on our Behind the Idea podcast this week as a comparison to Amazon ( AMZN ).
The key difference is that content and entertainment seems to be a much less cyclical and macro-exposed sector than home buying and selling. Netflix also has more obvious pricing power. I'm not sure the segment matters that much yet for Zillow, but it's also not clear it's a huge winner.
As far as the main business, the author's points that there's some overreaction embedded in here is probably fair. But the question comes back to price. Zillow now trades at 4.5x EV/sales, has no net income, and has decent free cash flow numbers but that are largely positive because we add back share-based compensation into cash flow. This is a question I'll ask again below, but how do we adjust for that properly?
Sentiment Check - Our author base is more bullish than not - I count one short idea this year vs. a few bullish authors and a few mixed articles. This is a good article on what the house flipping play may actually be for Zillow.
Twilio: Another Beat And Raise Quarter Sets 2019 Up Nicely by Individual Investing Ideas Twilio: An 'Overvalued' Stock That Isn't Overvalued by Bert Hochfeld Twilio ( TWLO ) hasn't sold off meaningfully this year. In fact it hit a new 52-week high after its earnings two weeks ago, before pulling back just a little. So it's not in the wash-out category.
These two articles make the case that Twilio is going to continue to grab land and expand, so perhaps the SaaS playbook hasn't stopped working everywhere. Individual Investing Ideas says the purchase of Sendgrid ( SEND ) is a good fit, and that the company deserves a premium multiple of 10-11x EV/Revenues, while Bert Hochfeld says there is a larger addressable market for TWLO than the market seems to give credit for.
The SaaS playbook, as best I can make it out, is that these companies build up a solid balance sheet through raising money and their IPO, achieve considerable growth in converting industries into online applications, develop business models that are subscription oriented or otherwise cash generative so at least they're break even on the cash flow statement, and then at some point they have such industry dominance that the margins come on the income statement. Twilio is still growing above 60%, they are close to free cash flow neutral (not factoring in share-based compensation or acquisitions), and nothing has changed in the story. I'm reminded of another point that Damodaran made in our podcast, towards the end, which is that you value companies based on the story they're telling. If Twilio's growth story continues to play out, some sort of premium will attach itself to the stock. I'm not very good at sussing out how high that premium should go, but the thesis hasn't broken across the board.
Sentiment Check - It's been a while since anyone has been bearish on Twilio, and comments lean quite bullish as well.
Sierra Wireless: Q3 Overreaction Creates An Opportunity by Stock-Picking Bartender Sierra Wireless ( SWIR ) is more on the semi-conductor side of the tech sector, and one that has never seemed to deliver for investors. Stock-Picking Bartender calls it out after a bad Q3 response because its business is shifting towards a recurring subscription model which, yes, makes it more like a software company. The company has achieved positive free cash flow this year and has grown revenue over time, and also has a clean balance sheet. So there are definite positives. But there is a track record (see the sentiment check) that suggests management has to prove they can achieve profitability and serious free cash flow with this shift.
Sentiment Check - This is our 5th bullish author on SWIR this year. Comments are mostly positive, though I thought this one nails the questions around the stock.
Yelp: It's Not Perfect, But At Least It's Cheap by Gary Alexander I've added Yelp ( YELP ) to my stock watch list for a few basic reasons:
Good revenue growth Clean balance sheet Online advertising appears likely to continue to be a growth business, and the sentiment and regulatory climate suggests Alphabet ( GOOG ) and especially Facebook ( FB ) will not reap all of the profits from the industry as they deal with other issues. I have a lot more reading to do, but I thought this article interesting as a place to start ("not perfect but at least cheap" could be pinned to value investors' walls around the world). Gary Alexander points out that the company is still expecting double-digit revenue growth in 2019, and that their lowered guidance and results in Q3/Q4 are due to a transition to non-term contracts and aftereffects (customers are no longer locked in for a minimum period, making it easier to sign new accounts but also to lose them). The big question beyond that transition for Yelp is whether it can hold its own against the big players.
The other question I have is around the share-based compensation, which again more or less matches the company's free cash flow. Is the right way to deal with this to just model an ever rising share count? Or to measure free cash flow after deducting the compensation and adding back proceeds from share option exercises? Something else? The company is spending considerable money on a buyback to prevent dilution, which further complicates this for me. Thoughts?
Sentiment Check - Comments lean bullish, and articles are also more bullish than not. There's a theme here.
PDFS: A Potential Turnaround Story by Goran Djukic This is one more 'traditional' tech company. PDF Solutions ( PDFS ) helps companies improve their "integrated circuit ("IC") design and manufacturing processes" ( source ), and so is heavily exposed to semiconductor cycles, which are not trending so hot right now. No surprise that PDFS's revenue is down 12% YTD, with most of the hit coming in Q3. Djukic points out that PDFS too is moving to a recurring revenue model, and perhaps there's some transition noise involved here. Or it could just be that the sector has been hit, and as long as PDFS can maintain share, they should do ok - there is over $96M in cash on the balance sheets, which may help investors sleep at night. Looks like an interesting idea for someone lurking in the semiconductor space.
Sentiment Check - This is our first idea on the stock this year. It has been pitched as a value play several times in the past. The one comment on the article is bullish about the company's expertise.
Three other ideas that caught my eye but that I can't write up in full:
Emperor Entertainment Hotel: A Weighted Coin by Brian Grosso - Hong Kong traded casino play. Off the usual SA radar, but interesting (note - this is a slideshow pitch) from a good author. Don't Shut The Frontdoor - Buy It by Cardon Capital - I wrote up Frontdoor ( FTDR ) before it spun off. After trading expensively, it has come down to more reasonable levels, if still above what I called a fair entry price pre-spin. I haven't revisited in full yet, but this is a good place to catch up on the stock, from a new author. Fraport: Much More Than Just Frankfurt's Airport by Silver Coast Research - I own shares in two different airport companies (note - not doing so great!), and am always interested in reading more. Silver Coast Research covers the sector regularly and well. Short ideas We published 19 short ideas in the week in question. You won't be surprised that Tesla ( TSLA ) comes up in three cases, but you might be that we published three updates on a Trupanion ( TRUP ) short idea. I've covered that before here, but here are three other short ideas that are at least related to modern technology.
Square's Valuation Problem by Mark Hake Square ( SQ ) is the most obvious tech company of this group, and is still comfortably a large cap. This article is very cut and dry in its analysis, and almost an exact flipside of the Twilio pieces. Hake points out that the numbers don't justify buying shares. He doesn't do a long analysis of TAM or where the revenue might go in the long term. He points out margins aren't attractive yet. And he takes peer multiples, gives SQ credit for meaningful growth in coming years, and says we're still short of the mark. The same questions apply - what is the long-term story for SQ, how does that relate to value over time, and how should we assess the company accordingly?
Sentiment Check - Comments reflect the SaaS playbook - growth is what matters, this is a reasonable multiple considering, and so forth. Another author takes the other side of the trade and gets a little more granular in SQ's business.
The Real Story Behind ElectraMeccanica by Vincent Ventures As if Tesla isn't enough, we have a short idea on ElectraMeccanica ( SOLO ), a company that makes three-wheeled electric cars. Dropping a wheel doesn't absolve the company from scrutiny, and Vincent Ventures raises questions about the CEO's background and commitment, as well as the company's financials. This doesn't appear to be a particularly contentious story, but it is worth checking out.
Sentiment Check - Comments mostly support the author's thesis. We have two bullish authors on the stock earlier in the year, and just this week Vincent Ventures followed up on their thesis and another author raised questions about SOLO's eligibility for US subsidies.
The C-Band Alliance - A Proposal In Trouble by Paul Litchfield Intelsat ( I ) is also loosely in the tech sector, and we looked at the Kerrisdale long thesis on the company and the short thesis pushback from Litchfield back in June. Litchfield updates his side of the case here, arguing that there's little chance the FCC will accept a key proposal for Intelsat's clearing of spectrum. There are a lot of details, so I won't get into it here, but it looks like a compelling argument.
Sentiment Check - Sentiment has quieted down, with this being the first article since August. Comments support the author's view here.
***
That's it for today's Idea Guide. As always, thanks for reading. This is a newsletter published exclusively to Essential and PRO+ subscribers. If you click to follow and get real-time alerts, you will get this in your email inbox. We've been publishing twice a week, though it's possible the schedule may switch to weekly for the rest of the year. Watch out for another Idea Guide on Friday catching up on Thanksgiving week ideas.
If you have any favorite ideas, suggestions, or corrections, comment below or send me a direct message , or email me at daniel@seekingalpha.com . I would love to hear how to make this more useful for you.
Have a Happy Thanksgiving to all those celebrating!
